sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know *aunque* from A2 Unit 28: the indicative for a fact, the subjunctive for a possibility (Lesson 1 of this unit). *Aun cuando* "even when, even if" follows exactly the same rule, but it is more formal and sounds more emphatic. You hear it in speeches and read it in essays and news, when someone promises to do something in spite of a difficulty.

sections.title: Aun cuando: fact or possibility
rows: Aun cuando sea difícil, hay que decir la verdad.
Even if it is difficult, you have to tell the truth. (A possibility: subjunctive.)
Aun cuando tenía miedo, habló delante de todos.
Even though he was afraid, he spoke in front of everyone. (A fact: indicative.)
El museo abrirá aun cuando llueva.
The museum will open even if it rains. (A possibility: subjunctive.)
Aunque sea difícil, hay que decir la verdad.
The everyday version of the first sentence, with *aunque*.

sections.title: Register and spelling
sections.content: In everyday speech, *aunque* is enough. *Aun cuando* adds weight, so it suits a serious promise or a firm position. You can swap *aunque* for *aun cuando* in the sentences above, but not the other way round in a casual chat, where it would sound stiff. Write *aun* without an accent in *aun cuando*. With an accent, *aún* means "still" (*aún no ha llegado*).

items.spanish: Aun cuando sea difícil, vamos a decir la verdad.
items.english: Even if it is difficult, we are going to tell the truth.

items.spanish: Vamos a seguir adelante aun cuando haya problemas.
items.english: We are going to carry on even if there are problems.

items.spanish: Aun cuando tenía miedo, habló delante de todos.
items.english: Even though he was afraid, he spoke in front of everyone.

items.spanish: El museo abrirá aun cuando llueva.
items.english: The museum will open even if it rains.

sections.content: The mood works just as with *aunque*. Ask whether the speaker presents the obstacle as a real fact (indicative) or as something possible that will not change the plan (subjunctive). After a past verb, a possible obstacle uses the imperfect subjunctive from B1 Unit 38.
